extracted.intended_audience: historians/demographers/anthropologists estimating early-19th-century California aboriginal populations
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and evaluative principles for reconstructing pre-contact and early‑19th‑century aboriginal population sizes in the Tulare Lake and Kaweah basins, using documentary, missionary, archaeological, and observational sources with explicit corrections and assumptions. Focuses on how to interpret, correct, and combine disparate historical counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children proportion assumption (15%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The children constituted between 10 and 20 per cent of the aboriginal population; "it is wholly reasonable to establish the arbitrary figure of 15 per cent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 15% as an operational value to compute total population from reported counts of children (example: applying 15% to Martin's count of 200 children at Bubal yields ~1,333 persons). Document the arbitrariness and uncertainty of this assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission census children percentage (21.4%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the missions the annual censuses (1782–1832) show individuals under ten years averaged 21.4% of the total population (Cook, 1940).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this mission-derived percentage as an upper-bound or check, but note it may be relatively high and not representative of gentile/aboriginal communities outside missions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archaeological age-profile evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Skeletal samples from habitation sites show age-at-death distributions (e.g., 22.6% dying under age 20 and perhaps 10–15% under age 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archaeological age distributions as an independent cross-check on age-group proportions from documentary sources; they may better reflect gentile conditions than mission records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment for disturbed sex ratio (set men = women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Captured natives brought to missions distort the sex ratio; the natural sex ratio was likely nearly unity. "We are justified in setting the number of men equal to that of the women."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mission or conversion records show a skewed sex ratio, adjust by assuming parity (e.g., the 5,217 conversions become 5,626 when men set equal to women). Note rationale (men slain/escaped) and document adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of baptism/mission records distinguishing men/women/children
rubrics_metrics.description: Baptism records that list gentile baptisms by village and distinguish men, women, and children provide composition data (example: 5,217 baptisms with 17.8% children, 37.1% men).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit mission baptism records to compute proportions and sex ratios, but account for capture/selection bias of the sample and correct where indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Largest estimates favored when fugitivism/absences bias counts low
rubrics_metrics.description: Because explorers often reported that inhabitants fled or were absent, "the largest estimates are likely to have been the most accurate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accounts note flight or partial absence, prefer higher contemporary estimates (or adjust low counts upward) since many observers saw only a residue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply a correction factor to Moraga–Munoz data (x2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moraga (Munoz diary) consistently underestimated populations because figures were based on those seen (often after flight) or gentile statements; "the figures should be regarded as indicating only about 50 per cent of the true population."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless specific reason otherwise, double Moraga–Munoz counts (apply correction factor of 2) to approximate true aboriginal numbers. Do not apply this correction to more careful observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer careful/precise observers (Cabot, Estudillo) over casual ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Some visitors (e.g., Cabot, Estudillo) made careful counts and are far more reliable than others (e.g., Moraga/Munoz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight counts by observer quality: trust detailed counts and methodical observers and avoid applying blanket corrections to their figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use heads-of-family counts with assumed family size
rubrics_metrics.description: When sources report heads of families, multiply by an assumed household size to get totals (example: 300 heads * 4 persons = 1,200).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a plausible average family size (the author used four) to convert household counts into total population, and state the assumed multiplier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer totals from counts of specific categories (warriors/young men) using ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of warriors or young men can be extrapolated to total population by applying the observed ratio of young men to total (example: Estudillo's 437 warriors + 600 women/children -> use ratio to infer totals; 600 young men represented ~1,700 persons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive or borrow a young-men:total ratio from closely observed villages (e.g., Chischa) and apply it to similar counts in the same district, with caution about visitor composition effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign numerical values to qualitative descriptors (e.g., 'big rancheria' ~ several hundred)
rubrics_metrics.description: When documents use qualitative descriptors like 'big rancheria' without numbers, infer a numerical value (author uses several hundred; example: assume 500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate qualitative size descriptors into plausible numeric estimates using regional village-size scales; document the choice and sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrapolation and area comparisons when direct evidence lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Where later informants or documentary evidence are unavailable or unreliable (e.g., post-1900), fall back upon extrapolation and comparisons among areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare analogous areas and use spatial/demographic analogies to estimate missing values; fully document assumptions and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for refugees/fugitives distribution (usually negligible concentration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fugitives reported by missions were widely distributed; "It is highly unlikely that as many as 300 would be concentrated at one village such as Bubal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mission reports cite cumulative fugitives, assume they were dispersed rather than concentrated in one village unless evidence indicates otherwise; avoid over-attributing refugees to single settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider migration, temporary scattering, and relocation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Villages were often deserted or inhabitants fled to swamps/islands; such movement affects contemporary counts (e.g., people fled into the lake and made temporary settlements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret single-visit counts in light of mobility: a low count may reflect temporary absence or relocation rather than true low population. Use multiple dated accounts to trace movements and adjust estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor in war, famine, and disease as causes of attrition
rubrics_metrics.description: War, disease (epidemic), and starvation greatly reduced populations; documented periods of 'mortandad' and repeated raids imply drastic declines (e.g., 50% decrease over a decade not surprising).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat observed post-contact counts as likely underestimates of pre-contact numbers and, where appropriate, apply reduction/restore factors or explicitly state that later counts reflect attrition rather than original size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use village area and measured dimensions to cross-check counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured village dimensions (e.g., Chischa: area 80,000 square varas) and mapping to familiar units (city blocks) provide cross-checks of plausible population given assumed densities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine measured area with plausible household spacing and population densities to corroborate or question verbal counts; use spatial geometry and unit conversions carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer tribe totals by summing principal village plus estimated satellites (fractional assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When tribe-level totals are needed and only principal village sizes known, estimate other villages as fractions (example: assume three other villages each half size of principal one -> tribe total computed accordingly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the fraction used (author used one-half for subsidiary villages) and justify by ethnographic evidence such as number of named villages and comparative scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret documentary language for epidemiological meaning ('mortandad' -> epidemic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used by Spanish/Mexican writers, such as 'mortandad,' were widely employed to connote effects of an epidemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read historical terms in context and treat certain words as evidence of disease outbreaks; use that inference to explain sudden population declines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt conservative/arbitrary figures when exact values impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the exact value can never be ascertained, select reasonable arbitrary figures and proceed (author uses such choices when necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the arbitrariness, justify chosen values with cross-evidence, and report sensitivity (how totals change if assumptions vary).
